title: What Is Pilates?
description: Who started Pilates, what the method trains, and the main types: mat, reformer, chair and barrel. STOTT is only one teaching school.
primaryQuestion: What is Pilates, who started it, and what types are there?
directAnswer: Joseph Hubertus Pilates, born in Mönchengladbach in 1883, built the exercise method he called Contrology and introduced that system in the United States in the late 1920s. The NHS describes Pilates today as work for balance, posture, strength and flexibility. Types differ by format: mat work on the floor, and apparatus such as the reformer, trapeze table, chair and barrel. Classical teaching stays closer to his original order. Contemporary schools, including STOTT, adapt it. A class coaches movement. It does not examine you the way a physiotherapy visit does.

sections.heading: Who started Pilates
paragraphs: The Pilates Method Alliance records that Joseph Hubertus Pilates was born in Mönchengladbach, Germany, on 9 December 1883. He taught physical culture, created a system of corrective exercise, and introduced that system to the American market in the late 1920s. He named the work Contrology. He published Your Health in 1934 and Return to Life Through Contrology in 1945. He died in October 1967, aged 83. Clara Pilates continued teaching at their New York studio.

Dancers in New York trained with him, and the signature mat series took shape while he taught at Jacob’s Pillow between 1942 and 1947. That is history of the method, not evidence that a class today will repair an injury. In 2000 a US court held that Pilates is a generic name for this kind of exercise, so one company cannot own the word as a trademark.

sections.heading: What the method is meant to train
paragraphs: An NHS beginners video calls Pilates exercise for balance, posture, strength and flexibility, and says a basic session can suit a wide range of ages and fitness. The same page says those videos are general exercise. They are not aimed at treating one cause of pain or a named condition. Contrology, his own word, points to control of how you move, breathe and place the body. It is a teaching aim, not a promise that pain will stop.

A separate NHS page lists pilates with stretching, yoga and tai chi as flexibility activity. It also describes muscle-strengthening work on at least two days a week for the major muscle groups. That two-day pattern is general strength guidance. It is not a Pilates prescription, and it does not say a class will fix a bad back.

sections.heading: Mat work, the floor type
paragraphs: Mat Pilates uses the floor. Body weight supplies most of the load, and a teacher may add a small ring or band. Return to Life Through Contrology is the book that set out his mat series, so this type is the one people can most often try without a studio machine. Group classes and home videos are usually mat work.

A mat hour can still be hard. Advanced sequences ask for a lot of control. Learn a pattern with someone who can see you before you copy a long video alone. The NHS caution still applies: stop if it hurts, and get advice first if you are pregnant, newly postnatal, injured, or unsure.

sections.heading: Reformer, chair, barrel and other apparatus
paragraphs: The Universal Reformer is the apparatus most often linked with his name. It is a sliding carriage on springs, so the load can be lighter or heavier than body weight. The Pilates Method Alliance also lists apparatus he kept adding: the Trapeze Table, often called a Cadillac, the Wunda Chair, the Magic Circle, the Spine Corrector and the Ladder Barrel. Each one changes the support and the direction of the effort. They are types of equipment, not separate brands and not separate sports.

You do not need every machine to be doing Pilates. Many people only ever meet the mat or the reformer, because chairs and barrels are less common and usually need a studio. Cost, space and class size decide what is actually bookable. Ask which piece of equipment the session uses before you pay.

sections.heading: Classical teaching and later schools
paragraphs: Classical, or Contrology, teaching stays closer to Joseph Pilates’ original exercise order and to the apparatus he designed. Contemporary teaching keeps the exercises but uses later ideas about how joints and muscles are coached. Both can be mat or apparatus. The label tells you the school of teaching, not whether the hour is safe for you.

STOTT Pilates is one contemporary school, tied to Merrithew training. It is not the definition of Pilates, and this page does not rank it above other schools. How that school uses Mat and Reformer is explained on the STOTT page. If a timetable only says Pilates, ask whether it is classical or contemporary, mat or apparatus, and how a movement is changed when it does not suit you.

sections.heading: When a class is the wrong first step
paragraphs: The NHS beginners video says to get advice from a health professional first if you are unsure about your fitness, have an injury or symptoms, have had a recent operation or similar health event, or you are pregnant or recently gave birth. Stop straight away if you feel pain or become unwell. If symptoms worry you, call your own doctor, or local emergency services if they are severe.

Leaking urine, pelvic heaviness, or a new abdominal gap after birth are reasons to start with women’s health physiotherapy rather than any type of mixed class. Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) teaches Pilates, including STOTT Mat and Reformer, and she also assesses those symptoms. Joining her class is still a class, not that assessment.

faqs.question: Who invented Pilates?
faqs.answer: Joseph Hubertus Pilates, born in Germany in 1883, developed the method and called it Contrology. He introduced it in the United States in the late 1920s and published Return to Life Through Contrology in 1945. He died in 1967.

faqs.question: What types of Pilates are there?
faqs.answer: The usual split is mat work on the floor and apparatus work. Apparatus includes the reformer, trapeze table, Wunda chair and barrels. Classical teaching follows his original order more closely. Contemporary schools, such as STOTT, adapt the same idea.

faqs.question: Do I need a reformer to do Pilates?
faqs.answer: No. Mat sessions use the floor and are the most widely available type. A reformer changes the load with springs. Chairs and barrels are further equipment choices, not a requirement for the exercise to count as Pilates.

faqs.question: Is Pilates a treatment?
faqs.answer: No. NHS material presents it as general exercise for balance, posture, strength and flexibility, not as care for one diagnosis. Pain, leaks, pregnancy or a recent birth need advice before you join a class of any type.

corrections: Added Joseph Pilates, Contrology, and the apparatus types from the Pilates Method Alliance history page.
Kept STOTT as one contemporary school with its own page, not as the definition of Pilates.
Did not repeat Joseph Pilates’ own claims that the method would remove disease or injury, and did not treat the NHS two-day strength pattern as a class prescription.

sourcesChecked.title: History of Pilates
sourcesChecked.limitations: Professional-association history. It includes his reputation with dancers and later promotional language about wellbeing. Those are not used here as clinical outcome evidence.
sourcesChecked.recommendation: Names Joseph Hubertus Pilates, birth on 9 December 1883 in Mönchengladbach, Contrology, the late-1920s US introduction, Your Health (1934), Return to Life Through Contrology (1945), death in October 1967, and apparatus including the Universal Reformer, Trapeze Table, Wunda Chair, Magic Circle, Spine Corrector and Ladder Barrel. Also records the 2000 ruling that Pilates is a generic exercise name.
